problem: "followed at the order of a feast" is garbled (source: observed in the order of a feast, i.e. in arranging a dinner); "government of the State" should be lowercase state per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: In Europe we often carry the ideas and habits of private life into public affairs. Since we pass at once from the family circle to the government of the state, we can often be heard discussing the great interests of society in the same way we talk with our friends. The Americans, on the other hand, carry the habits of public life over into their private manners. In their country the jury system is brought into the games of schoolboys, and parliamentary rules are followed in arranging a feast.

problem: "preponderating importance" rendered "decisive importance", which is stronger than his claim (an overriding weight, not a decisive one).
replacement: I have observed that the maintenance of democratic institutions in the United States is due to the circumstances, the laws, and the manners of that country. *l Most Europeans know only the first of these three causes, and they tend to give it an overriding importance that it does not really have.

problem: Omission of "inexhaustible" in "more unexplored and inexhaustible riches"; "riches" weakened to "resources".
replacement: The territory of the Union offers a boundless field to human activity and inexhaustible materials for industry and labor. The passion for wealth takes the place of ambition, and the heat of faction is cooled by a sense of prosperity. But where in the world shall we find more fertile plains, mightier rivers, or more unexplored and inexhaustible riches than in South America?

problem: "for the lasting of democratic institutions" is awkward; "the laws very subordinate to the manners" sharpened to "count for very little next to the manners".
replacement: The manners of the Americans of the United States are, then, the real reason why that people alone, among the American nations, can sustain a democratic government. It is the influence of manners that produces the different degrees of order and prosperity that can be seen in the several Anglo-American democracies. Europe, therefore, exaggerates what the geographical position of a country can do for the durability of democratic institutions. It gives too much weight to legislation and too little to manners. These three great causes no doubt help to regulate and direct the American democracy. But if I had to rank them in their proper order, I would say that physical circumstances count for less than the laws, and the laws are very much subordinate to the manners of the people. I am convinced that the most favorable situation and the best possible laws cannot sustain a constitution against the manners of a country, while manners can turn even the most unfavorable situations and the worst laws to some advantage. The importance of manners is a common truth to which study and experience keep bringing us back. It may be regarded as the central point in the range of human observation, and the place where all inquiry finally ends. I insist on this point so seriously that, if I have failed to make the reader feel the great influence I attribute to the practical experience, the habits, the opinions, in short the manners of the Americans, on the survival of their institutions, then I have failed in the main object of my work.

problem: "They would have to be introduced prudently" turns his participial condition into a requirement; "State" for the political body should be lowercase "state".
replacement: First, it seems to me that we must carefully distinguish the institutions of the United States from democratic institutions in general. When I think about Europe, with its mighty nations, populous cities, and formidable armies, and with the complexity of its politics, I cannot suppose that even the Anglo-Americans could live in our hemisphere with their ideas, their religion, and their manners and not alter their laws considerably. But we can imagine a democratic nation organized differently from the American people. It is not impossible to conceive of a government truly founded on the will of the majority, in which the majority nevertheless holds back its natural leaning toward equality. For the sake of order and stability in the state, it would consent to give a family or an individual all the prerogatives of the executive. A democratic society might exist in which the forces of the nation were more centralized than they are in the United States. The people would then have a less direct and less irresistible influence on public affairs, and yet every citizen, invested with certain rights, would still take part, within his own sphere, in running the government. What I observed among the Anglo-Americans leads me to believe that democratic institutions of this kind, if prudently introduced so that they gradually blend with the habits and mingle with the opinions of the people, might survive in other countries besides America. If the laws of the United States were the only democratic laws one could imagine, or the most perfect, I would admit that their success proves nothing about the success of democratic institutions in general in a country less favored by nature. But the laws of America seem to me defective in several ways, and I can easily imagine others of the same general kind. So the particular advantages of that country do not prove that democratic institutions cannot succeed in a nation less favored by circumstances, if it is ruled by better laws.

problem: "havoc in the State" should be lowercase state (political body) per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: In America we find the same passions as in Europe, some arising from human nature, others from the democratic condition of society. Thus in the United States I found the restlessness of heart that is natural to men when all ranks are nearly equal and everyone has the same chance of rising. I found the democratic feeling of envy expressed in a thousand different forms. I saw that the people often showed, in the conduct of affairs, a perfect mixture of ignorance and presumption, and I concluded that in America men are subject to the same failings and the same absurdities as among ourselves. But when I looked at the state of society more closely, I soon discovered that the Americans had made great and successful efforts to counteract these imperfections of human nature and to correct the natural defects of democracy. Their various municipal laws seemed to me a way of keeping the ambition of the citizens within a narrow sphere, and of turning those same passions that might have wreaked havoc in the state to the good of the township or the parish. The American legislators have succeeded, to a certain extent, in setting the notion of rights against the feelings of envy; the stability of the religious world against the constant shifting of politics; the experience of the people against its theoretical ignorance; and its practical knowledge of business against the impatience of its desires.

problem: "Providence seems to will on the generations" is unnatural English for "to impose upon".
replacement: The manners and laws of the Americans are not the only ones that may suit a democratic people. But the Americans have shown that it would be wrong to despair of regulating democracy with the help of manners and laws. Suppose other nations take this general and fruitful idea from the Americans, without meaning to copy the particular way they have applied it. Suppose they try to prepare themselves for the social condition that Providence seems to impose on the generations of this age, and so to escape the despotism or the anarchy that threatens them. What reason is there to suppose that their efforts would fail? The organization and establishment of democracy in Christendom is the great political problem of the time. The Americans, unquestionably, have not solved this problem, but they supply useful data to those who undertake the task.

problem: "rulers of the State" should be lowercase state (political body) per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: But what remains now of those barriers that once stopped the aggressions of tyranny? Religion has lost its empire over the souls of men, so the most prominent boundary between good and evil has been overthrown. The very elements of the moral world are uncertain. The princes and the peoples of the earth are guided by chance, and no one can define the natural limits of despotism or the bounds of license. Long revolutions have destroyed forever the respect that once surrounded the rulers of the state. Now that they have been relieved of the burden of public esteem, princes may from now on give themselves up without fear to the temptations of arbitrary power.

problem: "But this is what I believe. Suppose we fail..." detaches his "I am of opinion" from the conditional and its consequence, so the consequence reads as flat assertion; restore the hedge's scope.
replacement: But I am of the opinion that if we do not succeed in gradually introducing democratic institutions into France, and if we give up hope of giving the citizens the ideas and feelings that first prepare them for freedom and then let them enjoy it, there will be no independence for anyone, whether the middle classes or the nobility, the poor or the rich, but an equal tyranny over all. And I foresee that if the peaceable empire of the majority is not established among us in time, we shall sooner or later arrive at the unlimited authority of a single despot.
